claim: Proteins persist longer in the fossil record than DNA.
source: Proteins persist longer in the fossil record than DNA, but the longevity, survival mechanisms and substrates remain contested.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: The longevity, survival mechanisms and substrates of proteins in the fossil record remain contested.
source: Proteins persist longer in the fossil record than DNA, but the longevity, survival mechanisms and substrates remain contested.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a current gap in knowledge.

claim: Mineral binding plays a role in preserving protein sequence in ostrich eggshell.
source: Here, we demonstrate the role of mineral binding in preserving the protein sequence in ostrich (Struthionidae) eggshell, including from the palaeontological sites of Laetoli (3.8 Ma) and Olduvai Gorge (1.3 Ma) in Tanzania.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data and molecular dynamics simulations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Protein sequences have been recovered from ostrich eggshell from Laetoli (3.8 Ma).
source: Here, we demonstrate the role of mineral binding in preserving the protein sequence in ostrich (Struthionidae) eggshell, including from the palaeontological sites of Laetoli (3.8 Ma) and Olduvai Gorge (1.3 Ma) in Tanzania.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in the results section and supplementary files.

claim: Protein sequences have been recovered from ostrich eggshell from Olduvai Gorge (1.3 Ma).
source: Here, we demonstrate the role of mineral binding in preserving the protein sequence in ostrich (Struthionidae) eggshell, including from the palaeontological sites of Laetoli (3.8 Ma) and Olduvai Gorge (1.3 Ma) in Tanzania.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in the results section and supplementary files.

claim: Consistent patterns of preservation are found when tracking protein diagenesis back in time.
source: By tracking protein diagenesis back in time we find consistent patterns of preservation, demonstrating authenticity of the surviving sequences.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid racemization data and LC-MS/MS analyses across samples of different ages shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Struthiocalcin-1 and struthiocalcin-2 are the dominant proteins within ostrich eggshell.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of struthiocalcin-1 and -2, the dominant proteins within the eggshell, reveal that distinct domains bind to the mineral surface.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic analysis of modern eggshell shown in Appendix 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Distinct domains of struthiocalcin-1 and -2 bind to the mineral surface.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of struthiocalcin-1 and -2, the dominant proteins within the eggshell, reveal that distinct domains bind to the mineral surface.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulations presented in Table 2 and Appendix 3.

claim: The domain with the strongest calculated binding energy to the calcite surface is selectively preserved.
source: It is the domain with the strongest calculated binding energy to the calcite surface that is selectively preserved.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between binding energy calculations (Table 2) and peptide survival data (Figure 3).

claim: The Laetoli and Olduvai peptides are 50 times older than any previously authenticated sequence in terms of thermal age.
source: Thermal age calculations demonstrate that the Laetoli and Olduvai peptides are 50 times older than any previously authenticated sequence (equivalent to ~16 Ma at a constant 10°C).
evidence: This is supported by thermal age calculations presented in Figure 1 and Appendix 1.

claim: The Laetoli and Olduvai peptides have a thermal age equivalent to ~16 Ma at a constant 10°C.
source: Thermal age calculations demonstrate that the Laetoli and Olduvai peptides are 50 times older than any previously authenticated sequence (equivalent to ~16 Ma at a constant 10°C).
evidence: This is supported by thermal age calculations presented in Figure 1 and Appendix 1.

claim: Ancient protein and DNA sequences are revolutionising our understanding of the past.
source: Ancient protein and DNA sequences are revolutionising our understanding of the past, providing information on phylogeny, migration, evolution, domestication and extinction (Hagelberg et al., 2015; Cappellini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: Ancient biomolecular sequences provide information on phylogeny, migration, evolution, domestication and extinction.
source: Ancient protein and DNA sequences are revolutionising our understanding of the past, providing information on phylogeny, migration, evolution, domestication and extinction (Hagelberg et al., 2015; Cappellini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: The absence of ancient biomolecular data from warm regions and deep time highlights the fragility of these biomolecules.
source: However, the absence of data from warm regions and deep time (Wade, 2015) highlights the fragility of these biomolecules and has so far hampered our ability to answer fundamental evolutionary questions, such as resolving the phylogenetic tree of the genus Homo in Africa.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wade (2015) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The absence of ancient biomolecular data from warm regions and deep time has hampered the ability to answer fundamental evolutionary questions.
source: However, the absence of data from warm regions and deep time (Wade, 2015) highlights the fragility of these biomolecules and has so far hampered our ability to answer fundamental evolutionary questions, such as resolving the phylogenetic tree of the genus Homo in Africa.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wade (2015) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Resolving the phylogenetic tree of the genus Homo in Africa is a fundamental evolutionary question that has been hampered by lack of ancient biomolecular data.
source: However, the absence of data from warm regions and deep time (Wade, 2015) highlights the fragility of these biomolecules and has so far hampered our ability to answer fundamental evolutionary questions, such as resolving the phylogenetic tree of the genus Homo in Africa.
evidence: This is an example provided in the text to illustrate the impact of the lack of ancient biomolecular data.

claim: The survival of proteins and DNA in tropical environments is deemed extremely unlikely.
source: The survival of proteins and DNA in tropical environments and in fossils that go back a few million years (Ma) is deemed extremely unlikely and therefore the impact of the 'biomolecular revolution' in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology has so far been relatively limited.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field prior to this study.

claim: The survival of proteins and DNA in fossils that go back a few million years is deemed extremely unlikely.
source: The survival of proteins and DNA in tropical environments and in fossils that go back a few million years (Ma) is deemed extremely unlikely and therefore the impact of the 'biomolecular revolution' in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology has so far been relatively limited.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field prior to this study.

claim: The impact of the 'biomolecular revolution' in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology has been relatively limited.
source: The survival of proteins and DNA in tropical environments and in fossils that go back a few million years (Ma) is deemed extremely unlikely and therefore the impact of the 'biomolecular revolution' in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology has so far been relatively limited.
evidence: This is presented as a consequence of the difficulty of recovering ancient biomolecules from warm regions and deep time.

claim: Claims for exceptional preservation in the fossil record have been put forward in a number of studies.
source: Claims for exceptional preservation in the fossil record have been put forward in a number of studies (Towe and Urbanek, 1972; Bertazzo et al., 2015; Schweitzer et al., 2013; Cleland et al., 2015), but these have not been satisfactorily substantiated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Previous claims for exceptional preservation in the fossil record have not been satisfactorily substantiated.
source: Claims for exceptional preservation in the fossil record have been put forward in a number of studies (Towe and Urbanek, 1972; Bertazzo et al., 2015; Schweitzer et al., 2013; Cleland et al., 2015), but these have not been satisfactorily substantiated.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of previous work in the field.

claim: Morphological evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils has been reported.
source: Morphological (Towe and Urbanek, 1972; Bertazzo et al., 2015), immunological (Schweitzer et al., 2013) and spectroscopic (Bertazzo et al., 2015) evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils seems to be inconsistent with the observed levels of hydrolysis, dehydration and racemization (Penkman et al., 2013) in intracrystalline proteins from the fossil mollusc shell (Sykes et al., 1995) and eggshell (Brooks et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Immunological evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils has been reported.
source: Morphological (Towe and Urbanek, 1972; Bertazzo et al., 2015), immunological (Schweitzer et al., 2013) and spectroscopic (Bertazzo et al., 2015) evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils seems to be inconsistent with the observed levels of hydrolysis, dehydration and racemization (Penkman et al., 2013) in intracrystalline proteins from the fossil mollusc shell (Sykes et al., 1995) and eggshell (Brooks et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spectroscopic evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils has been reported.
source: Morphological (Towe and Urbanek, 1972; Bertazzo et al., 2015), immunological (Schweitzer et al., 2013) and spectroscopic (Bertazzo et al., 2015) evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils seems to be inconsistent with the observed levels of hydrolysis, dehydration and racemization (Penkman et al., 2013) in intracrystalline proteins from the fossil mollusc shell (Sykes et al., 1995) and eggshell (Brooks et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs seems inconsistent with observed levels of hydrolysis, dehydration and racemization in intracrystalline proteins from fossil mollusc shell and eggshell.
source: Morphological (Towe and Urbanek, 1972; Bertazzo et al., 2015), immunological (Schweitzer et al., 2013) and spectroscopic (Bertazzo et al., 2015) evidence of preserved tissues in dinosaurs and other fossils seems to be inconsistent with the observed levels of hydrolysis, dehydration and racemization (Penkman et al., 2013) in intracrystalline proteins from the fossil mollusc shell (Sykes et al., 1995) and eggshell (Brooks et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of different lines of evidence cited from the literature.

claim: Crosslinking has been proposed as a mechanism that enhances the survival of ancient biomolecules.
source: The mechanisms that might allow preservation over palaeontological and geological time scales are also poorly understood: crosslinking, organo-metallic complexing, including with iron, compression/confinement (Logan et al., 1991; Schweitzer et al., 2014), and mineral stabilization (Collins et al., 2000) have all been proposed as mechanisms that enhance the survival of ancient biomolecules.
evidence: This is stated as one of several proposed mechanisms from the literature.

claim: Organo-metallic complexing, including with iron, has been proposed as a mechanism that enhances the survival of ancient biomolecules.
source: The mechanisms that might allow preservation over palaeontological and geological time scales are also poorly understood: crosslinking, organo-metallic complexing, including with iron, compression/confinement (Logan et al., 1991; Schweitzer et al., 2014), and mineral stabilization (Collins et al., 2000) have all been proposed as mechanisms that enhance the survival of ancient biomolecules.
evidence: This is stated as one of several proposed mechanisms from the literature.

claim: Compression/confinement has been proposed as a mechanism that enhances the survival of ancient biomolecules.
source: The mechanisms that might allow preservation over palaeontological and geological time scales are also poorly understood: crosslinking, organo-metallic complexing, including with iron, compression/confinement (Logan et al., 1991; Schweitzer et al., 2014), and mineral stabilization (Collins et al., 2000) have all been proposed as mechanisms that enhance the survival of ancient biomolecules.
evidence: This is stated as one of several proposed mechanisms from the literature.

claim: Mineral stabilization has been proposed as a mechanism that enhances the survival of ancient biomolecules.
source: The mechanisms that might allow preservation over palaeontological and geological time scales are also poorly understood: crosslinking, organo-metallic complexing, including with iron, compression/confinement (Logan et al., 1991; Schweitzer et al., 2014), and mineral stabilization (Collins et al., 2000) have all been proposed as mechanisms that enhance the survival of ancient biomolecules.
evidence: This is stated as one of several proposed mechanisms from the literature.

claim: The mechanisms that might allow preservation of biomolecules over palaeontological and geological time scales are poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms that might allow preservation over palaeontological and geological time scales are also poorly understood: crosslinking, organo-metallic complexing, including with iron, compression/confinement (Logan et al., 1991; Schweitzer et al., 2014), and mineral stabilization (Collins et al., 2000) have all been proposed as mechanisms that enhance the survival of ancient biomolecules.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Kinetic estimates of degradation rates were used to normalize numerical ages to thermal age.
source: Here we have used kinetic estimates of degradation rates of DNA (Allentoft et al., 2012), collagen in bones (Buckley et al., 2008), and intracrystalline amino acids (Crisp et al., 2013) to normalize their numerical (chronological) ages to thermal age (Wehmiller, 1977) (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Thermal age is a measure which enables comparison between ancient biomolecular targets by normalising them to an equivalent age at a constant temperature of 10°C.
source: Thermal age is a measure which enables simple comparison between ancient biomolecular targets by normalising them to an equivalent (thermal) age, allowing all samples to be treated as having experienced a constant temperature of 10°C.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: Samples from cooler sites have thermal ages younger than their geochronological age.
source: Thus samples from cooler sites, which experience slower rates of chemical reaction, will have thermal ages younger than their geochronological age, whilst samples from warmer sites will be thermally 'older'.
evidence: This is explained as a consequence of the thermal age calculation method.

claim: Samples from warmer sites will be thermally 'older' than their geochronological age.
source: Thus samples from cooler sites, which experience slower rates of chemical reaction, will have thermal ages younger than their geochronological age, whilst samples from warmer sites will be thermally 'older'.
evidence: This is explained as a consequence of the thermal age calculation method.

claim: Various factors can affect the effective diagenetic temperature experienced by a sample.
source: Various factors can affect the effective diagenetic temperature experienced by a sample (and therefore impact on its thermal age), from burial depth to seasonal and interglacial / glacial cycles (Wehmiller, 1977; Huang et al., 2000; Eischeid et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Burial depth can affect the effective diagenetic temperature experienced by a sample.
source: Various factors can affect the effective diagenetic temperature experienced by a sample (and therefore impact on its thermal age), from burial depth to seasonal and interglacial / glacial cycles (Wehmiller, 1977; Huang et al., 2000; Eischeid et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Seasonal and interglacial/glacial cycles can affect the effective diagenetic temperature experienced by a sample.
source: Various factors can affect the effective diagenetic temperature experienced by a sample (and therefore impact on its thermal age), from burial depth to seasonal and interglacial / glacial cycles (Wehmiller, 1977; Huang et al., 2000; Eischeid et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The greatest absolute ages for recovered DNA are from high latitudes.
source: The greatest absolute ages for recovered DNA (Orlando et al., 2013) (0.7 Ma = 0.08 Ma@10°C) and for protein (Rybczynski, 2013) (3.5 Ma = 0.3 Ma@10°C) sequences are from high latitudes and their survival is consistent with predictions from the kinetic data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orlando et al., 2013.

claim: The oldest recovered DNA is 0.7 Ma old with a thermal age of 0.08 Ma@10°C.
source: The greatest absolute ages for recovered DNA (Orlando et al., 2013) (0.7 Ma = 0.08 Ma@10°C) and for protein (Rybczynski, 2013) (3.5 Ma = 0.3 Ma@10°C) sequences are from high latitudes and their survival is consistent with predictions from the kinetic data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orlando et al., 2013.

claim: The greatest absolute ages for recovered protein sequences are from high latitudes.
source: The greatest absolute ages for recovered DNA (Orlando et al., 2013) (0.7 Ma = 0.08 Ma@10°C) and for protein (Rybczynski, 2013) (3.5 Ma = 0.3 Ma@10°C) sequences are from high latitudes and their survival is consistent with predictions from the kinetic data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rybczynski, 2013.

claim: The oldest recovered protein sequence is 3.5 Ma old with a thermal age of 0.3 Ma@10°C.
source: The greatest absolute ages for recovered DNA (Orlando et al., 2013) (0.7 Ma = 0.08 Ma@10°C) and for protein (Rybczynski, 2013) (3.5 Ma = 0.3 Ma@10°C) sequences are from high latitudes and their survival is consistent with predictions from the kinetic data.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rybczynski, 2013.

claim: The survival of ancient DNA and protein from high latitudes is consistent with predictions from kinetic data.
source: The greatest absolute ages for recovered DNA (Orlando et al., 2013) (0.7 Ma = 0.08 Ma@10°C) and for protein (Rybczynski, 2013) (3.5 Ma = 0.3 Ma@10°C) sequences are from high latitudes and their survival is consistent with predictions from the kinetic data.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of observed data with kinetic predictions.

claim: The oldest protein-preserving sample from temperate latitudes is from Weybourne Crag (1.5 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C).
source: Younger samples from more temperate latitudes will have greater thermal ages, yet the oldest of these which has preserved protein (Weybourne Crag: 1.5 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C) has a thermal age similar to that of Middle Pleistocene DNA at Sima de los Huesos (0.4 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C) (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison point for thermal ages.

claim: Middle Pleistocene DNA from Sima de los Huesos is 0.4 Ma old with a thermal age of 0.2 Ma@10°C.
source: Younger samples from more temperate latitudes will have greater thermal ages, yet the oldest of these which has preserved protein (Weybourne Crag: 1.5 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C) has a thermal age similar to that of Middle Pleistocene DNA at Sima de los Huesos (0.4 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C) (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2014.

claim: Weybourne Crag protein has a thermal age similar to that of Middle Pleistocene DNA at Sima de los Huesos.
source: Younger samples from more temperate latitudes will have greater thermal ages, yet the oldest of these which has preserved protein (Weybourne Crag: 1.5 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C) has a thermal age similar to that of Middle Pleistocene DNA at Sima de los Huesos (0.4 Ma = 0.2 Ma@10°C) (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of thermal ages from different samples.

claim: Ostrich eggshell is abundant in archaeological and palaeontological sites throughout Africa.
source: Here we explore the impact of strong protein binding in biominerals and its effect on sequence survival, by targeting ancient ostrich eggshell (Struthio camelus; Struthioniformes), which is abundant in archaeological and palaeontological sites throughout Africa (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for choosing ostrich eggshell as the study material.

claim: The intracrystalline proteins were isolated and characterised from ostrich eggshell.
source: We isolated and characterised the intracrystalline proteins (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Appendix 2) and tracked their diagenesis back in time to 3.8 Ma ago.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Appendix 2.

claim: Protein diagenesis was tracked back in time to 3.8 Ma ago.
source: We isolated and characterised the intracrystalline proteins (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Appendix 2) and tracked their diagenesis back in time to 3.8 Ma ago.
evidence: This is supported by data from samples of different ages analyzed in the study.

claim: A systematic approach was used to validate the sequences from each eggshell sample.
source: Using a systematic approach, we validated the sequences from each of the eggshell samples analysed using amino acid racemization (AAR), organic volatile compounds, ancient DNA and proteomic analyses.
evidence: This is described as the methodological approach and is supported by data in multiple sections and appendices.

claim: Amino acid racemization was used to validate the sequences from eggshell samples.
source: Using a systematic approach, we validated the sequences from each of the eggshell samples analysed using amino acid racemization (AAR), organic volatile compounds, ancient DNA and proteomic analyses.
evidence: This is supported by AAR data presented in Figure 2 and Appendix 4.

claim: Organic volatile compounds were used to validate the sequences from eggshell samples.
source: Using a systematic approach, we validated the sequences from each of the eggshell samples analysed using amino acid racemization (AAR), organic volatile compounds, ancient DNA and proteomic analyses.
evidence: This is supported by volatile organic compound analysis described in Appendix 5, Section E.

claim: Ancient DNA analysis was used to validate the sequences from eggshell samples.
source: Using a systematic approach, we validated the sequences from each of the eggshell samples analysed using amino acid racemization (AAR), organic volatile compounds, ancient DNA and proteomic analyses.
evidence: This is supported by ancient DNA analysis described in Appendix 5, Section F.

claim: Proteomic analyses were used to validate the sequences from eggshell samples.
source: Using a systematic approach, we validated the sequences from each of the eggshell samples analysed using amino acid racemization (AAR), organic volatile compounds, ancient DNA and proteomic analyses.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data presented throughout the results section.

claim: Results are supported by in-depth analysis of patterns of diagenesis in both samples and blanks.
source: All our results are supported by in-depth analysis of patterns of diagenesis in both samples and blanks as well as the evaluation of potential contamination and carry-over.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 4 and Appendix 5.

claim: Results are supported by evaluation of potential contamination and carry-over.
source: All our results are supported by in-depth analysis of patterns of diagenesis in both samples and blanks as well as the evaluation of potential contamination and carry-over.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 4 showing blank analyses and carry-over assessment.

claim: Both hydrolysis and racemization increase with time in fossil eggshell samples.
source: For fossil eggshell samples the extent of degradation, quantified by chiral amino acid analysis (AAR), shows that both hydrolysis and racemization increase with time, and that racemic equilibrium is reached in samples older than 1 Ma (~3.6 Ma@10°C; Figure 2; and Appendix 4—table 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by AAR data shown in Figure 2 and Appendix 4.

claim: Racemic equilibrium is reached in eggshell samples older than 1 Ma (~3.6 Ma@10°C).
source: For fossil eggshell samples the extent of degradation, quantified by chiral amino acid analysis (AAR), shows that both hydrolysis and racemization increase with time, and that racemic equilibrium is reached in samples older than 1 Ma (~3.6 Ma@10°C; Figure 2; and Appendix 4—table 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by AAR data shown in Figure 2 and Appendix 4.

claim: As degradation proceeds, the complexity of the proteome decreases.
source: As degradation proceeds, the complexity of the proteome decreases, until only SCA-1 and SCA-2 are detected by LC-MS/MS in the oldest samples (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Only SCA-1 and SCA-2 are detected by LC-MS/MS in the oldest samples.
source: As degradation proceeds, the complexity of the proteome decreases, until only SCA-1 and SCA-2 are detected by LC-MS/MS in the oldest samples (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3.

claim: SCA-1 and SCA-2 are extremely well preserved in samples up to 150,000 years old.
source: These two proteins are extremely well preserved in samples up to 150,000 years old, but by 3.8 Ma few peptides are recovered (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3 and its supplements.

claim: By 3.8 Ma few peptides are recovered from SCA-1 and SCA-2.
source: These two proteins are extremely well preserved in samples up to 150,000 years old, but by 3.8 Ma few peptides are recovered (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3 and its supplements.

claim: A total of 22 peptide sequences was recovered from SCA-1 & SCA-2 in samples from Laetoli.
source: A total of 22 peptide sequences was recovered from SCA-1 & SCA-2 in samples from Laetoli (Appendix 5, section A; Supplementary file 2), consistent with the idea that dehydration, in addition to mineral binding, may also play a role in retarding degradation of non-binding peptides (Collins and Riley, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 5, section A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Dehydration, in addition to mineral binding, may play a role in retarding degradation of non-binding peptides.
source: A total of 22 peptide sequences was recovered from SCA-1 & SCA-2 in samples from Laetoli (Appendix 5, section A; Supplementary file 2), consistent with the idea that dehydration, in addition to mineral binding, may also play a role in retarding degradation of non-binding peptides (Collins and Riley, 2000).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis consistent with the data and supported by citation.

claim: 80% of the spectra consistently identified in Laetoli samples were assigned to charged species containing the four Asp residues found in the peptide YSALDDDDYPKG.
source: However, 80% of the spectra, consistently identified in ten independent LC-MS/MS analyses of three ostrich eggshell samples from Laetoli were assigned to charged species that contained the four Asp residues found in the peptide YSALDDDDYPKG.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data from ten independent analyses.

claim: The survival of the Asp-rich peptide region is not limited to samples from Laetoli.
source: The survival of this Asp-rich peptide region is not limited to the samples from Laetoli; the eggshells from Olduvai (~16 Ma@10°C) and Wonderwerk (~3.6 Ma@10°C) also show that this region of SCA-1 is preferentially preserved.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data from Olduvai and Wonderwerk samples shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eggshells from Olduvai show that the DDDD-containing region of SCA-1 is preferentially preserved.
source: The survival of this Asp-rich peptide region is not limited to the samples from Laetoli; the eggshells from Olduvai (~16 Ma@10°C) and Wonderwerk (~3.6 Ma@10°C) also show that this region of SCA-1 is preferentially preserved.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data from Olduvai samples shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eggshells from Wonderwerk show that the DDDD-containing region of SCA-1 is preferentially preserved.
source: The survival of this Asp-rich peptide region is not limited to the samples from Laetoli; the eggshells from Olduvai (~16 Ma@10°C) and Wonderwerk (~3.6 Ma@10°C) also show that this region of SCA-1 is preferentially preserved.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data from Wonderwerk samples shown in Figure 3.

claim: The DDDD-containing peptide does not survive in the absence of the mineral.
source: This peptide does not survive in the absence of the mineral, as shown by the artificial degradation experiments we conducted on purified eggshell proteins heated at 140°C in water (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Appendix 4, sections B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heated protein samples shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The same region of SCA-1 containing DDDD was too flexible to be determined when the crystallographic structure of pure SCA-1 was solved.
source: Indeed, the same region of the protein was too flexible to be determined when the crystallographic structure of pure SCA-1 was solved (Ruiz-Arellano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the crystallographic study.

claim: The patterns of degradation of proteins heated in water differ significantly from those after demineralisation of the eggshell mineral.
source: The patterns of degradation of the same proteins heated in water vs after demineralisation of the eggshell mineral also differ significantly from each other.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hydropathicity calculated for surviving peptides decreases in eggshell mineral.
source: It is noteworthy that the hydropathicity calculated for the surviving peptides decreases in eggshell mineral and increases in water (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the hypothesis that mineral binding plays a crucial role in the survival of selected peptide sequences.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hydropathicity calculated for surviving peptides increases in water.
source: It is noteworthy that the hydropathicity calculated for the surviving peptides decreases in eggshell mineral and increases in water (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the hypothesis that mineral binding plays a crucial role in the survival of selected peptide sequences.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in hydropathicity patterns is consistent with the hypothesis that mineral binding plays a crucial role in the survival of selected peptide sequences.
source: It is noteworthy that the hydropathicity calculated for the surviving peptides decreases in eggshell mineral and increases in water (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the hypothesis that mineral binding plays a crucial role in the survival of selected peptide sequences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of hydropathicity data.

claim: The amino acid concentration in procedural blanks was negligible.
source: The amino acid concentration was analysed in all bleached eggshell samples and controls (procedural blanks); concentrations in the blanks were negligible, while the samples retain the original organic fraction within the intracrystalline environment (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The samples retain the original organic fraction within the intracrystalline environment.
source: The amino acid concentration was analysed in all bleached eggshell samples and controls (procedural blanks); concentrations in the blanks were negligible, while the samples retain the original organic fraction within the intracrystalline environment (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid concentration data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The presence of volatile organic compounds in 2.7 Ma ostrich eggshell demonstrates the stability of ostrich eggshell as a closed system.
source: In addition, the presence of volatile organic compounds in 2.7 Ma ostrich eggshell demonstrates the stability of ostrich eggshell as a closed system (Appendix 5, Section E).
evidence: This is supported by volatile organic compound analysis described in Appendix 5, Section E.

claim: Ratite eggshell has previously proven to be an excellent source of ancient DNA.
source: Ratite eggshell has previously proven to be an excellent source of ancient DNA (Oskam et al., 2010) but, unsurprisingly, NGS sequencing failed to recover avian DNA from the Laetoli eggshell we tested (Appendix 5, Section F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oskam et al., 2010.

claim: NGS sequencing failed to recover avian DNA from the Laetoli eggshell.
source: Ratite eggshell has previously proven to be an excellent source of ancient DNA (Oskam et al., 2010) but, unsurprisingly, NGS sequencing failed to recover avian DNA from the Laetoli eggshell we tested (Appendix 5, Section F).
evidence: This is supported by ancient DNA analysis described in Appendix 5, Section F.

claim: Water blanks were injected between each LC-MS/MS eggshell sample analysis to assess carry-over.
source: Water blanks were injected between each LC-MS/MS eggshell sample analysis to assess carry-over (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Low levels of SCA-1 were occasionally detected in some of the blanks.
source: Despite low levels of SCA-1 being occasionally detected in some of the blanks (Figure 4D), the effective carry-over from sample to sample can be estimated to be below 0.01%.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The effective carry-over from sample to sample can be estimated to be below 0.01%.
source: Despite low levels of SCA-1 being occasionally detected in some of the blanks (Figure 4D), the effective carry-over from sample to sample can be estimated to be below 0.01%.
evidence: This is an estimate based on analysis of blank data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each batch of fossil eggshell was analysed separately in time.
source: We also stress that each batch of fossil eggshell was analysed separately in time (Figure 4C) and that therefore carry-over between younger and older eggshell samples is impossible.
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the timeline shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Carry-over between younger and older eggshell samples is impossible.
source: We also stress that each batch of fossil eggshell was analysed separately in time (Figure 4C) and that therefore carry-over between younger and older eggshell samples is impossible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal separation of analyses shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Independent analyses of the results in a second laboratory (Copenhagen) demonstrated the replicability of the results.
source: Finally, independent analyses of the results in a second laboratory (Copenhagen) also demonstrated the replicability of our results (Appendix 5, Section A).
evidence: This is supported by independent replication data described in Appendix 5, Section A.

claim: All peptides and proteins detected presented damage patterns consistent with the age of the samples.
source: All peptides and proteins detected in this study presented damage patterns (i.e. diagenesis-induced modifications, such as deamidation, oxidation) that are entirely consistent with the age of the samples (Appendix 5, Section D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of post-translational modifications described in Appendix 5, Section D and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The breakdown of proteins and peptides should primarily occur via hydrolysis.
source: The breakdown of the proteins and peptides should primarily occur via hydrolysis, involving water and proteins or peptides as reactants.
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge about protein degradation.

claim: The rate-determining step in protein hydrolysis is the attack of a water molecule.
source: The rate-determining step is the attack of a water molecule (or molecules, see Pan et al., 2011 for an extended discussion).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2011 and represents established chemical knowledge.

claim: The mechanism allowing survival of ancient sequences over ~4 Ma at equatorial sites is the stabilization of optimally configured peptides and associated water molecules by surface binding.
source: We argue that the mechanism allowing the survival of the ancient sequences over ~4 Ma (~16 Ma@10°C) at equatorial sites is the stabilization of optimally configured peptides and associated water molecules by surface binding at this interface.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by molecular dynamics simulations and experimental data.

claim: The low, negative free energy of binding means that amino acid residues will readily bind to the calcite surface and remain bound indefinitely.
source: The low, negative free energy of binding (Table 2) of the amino acid residues means that they will readily bind to the calcite surface and remain bound indefinitely and this binding stabilizes the peptides by lowering their configurational energy (Table 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on binding energy calculations shown in Table 2.

claim: Peptide binding stabilizes the peptides by lowering their configurational energy.
source: The low, negative free energy of binding (Table 2) of the amino acid residues means that they will readily bind to the calcite surface and remain bound indefinitely and this binding stabilizes the peptides by lowering their configurational energy (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by binding energy calculations shown in Table 2.

claim: The binding of the peptide forces the hydrolysis reaction to take place with the stabilized water close to the calcite surface.
source: The binding of the peptide also forces the hydrolysis reaction to take place with the stabilized water close to the calcite surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular dynamics simulations and the proposed mechanism.

claim: The presence of the calcite surface significantly stabilizes the water molecules surrounding the peptide.
source: Furthermore, the presence of the calcite surface significantly stabilizes the water molecules surrounding the peptide.
evidence: This is supported by residence time and diffusion calculations from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Table 2.

claim: Water molecules trapped between the protein and mineral surface have greater residence times than water molecules on the surface with no protein present.
source: Estimates of the residence times (Table 2) and diffusion values of water molecules trapped between the protein and mineral surface indicate that these water molecules have greater residence times and lower diffusion rates than water molecules on the surface with no protein present.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Table 2.

claim: Water molecules trapped between the protein and mineral surface have lower diffusion rates than water molecules on the surface with no protein present.
source: Estimates of the residence times (Table 2) and diffusion values of water molecules trapped between the protein and mineral surface indicate that these water molecules have greater residence times and lower diffusion rates than water molecules on the surface with no protein present.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Table 2.

claim: The stabilization of water molecules selectively lowers the ground state energy of the reactants at the interface with respect to the bulk.
source: This large stabilization of water molecules selectively lowers the ground state energy of the reactants (protein or peptide plus water) at the interface with respect to the bulk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular dynamics simulations and thermodynamic principles.

claim: The energy barrier for hydrolysis will be significantly larger for the bound protein or peptide than for the unbound one.
source: Thus the energy barrier will be significantly larger for the bound protein or peptide than for the unbound one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stabilization of reactants at the mineral surface.

claim: Surface molecules would need more energy (i.e. a higher temperature) to overcome the augmented barrier to hydrolysis.
source: Our surface molecules would therefore need more energy in the system (i.e. a higher temperature) to overcome the augmented barrier.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased energy barrier for hydrolysis of bound peptides.

claim: The net effect of peptide binding is to retard hydrolysis and prolong peptide sequence survival.
source: The net effect of the binding of the protein or peptide is therefore to retard hydrolysis and prolong peptide sequence survival, albeit of a select (mineral-binding) region of the protein.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion supported by both computational and experimental data.

claim: Only select (mineral-binding) regions of the protein have prolonged survival.
source: The net effect of the binding of the protein or peptide is therefore to retard hydrolysis and prolong peptide sequence survival, albeit of a select (mineral-binding) region of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by the selective preservation of the DDDD-containing peptide shown in Figure 3.

claim: Water molecules at the calcite surface would be expected to operate as if they were 'cooler' in terms of reactivity and rates of peptide bond hydrolysis.
source: This is effectively equivalent to a localised 'cooling' effect: the water molecules at the calcite surface would therefore be expected to operate as if they were 'cooler' in terms of reactivity and rates of peptide bond hydrolysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stabilization of water molecules at the mineral surface.

claim: The survival of 3.8 Ma old peptide sequences in equatorial Africa corresponds to an estimated thermal age of ~16 Ma@10°C.
source: The survival of 3.8 Ma old peptide sequences in equatorial Africa corresponds to an estimated thermal age of ~16 Ma@10°C, two orders of magnitude beyond the oldest recovered DNA (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by thermal age calculations shown in Figure 1 and Appendix 1.

claim: The thermal age of the 3.8 Ma peptide sequences is two orders of magnitude beyond the oldest recovered DNA.
source: The survival of 3.8 Ma old peptide sequences in equatorial Africa corresponds to an estimated thermal age of ~16 Ma@10°C, two orders of magnitude beyond the oldest recovered DNA (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison based on thermal age calculations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Surface stabilization of both the peptide and water molecules involved in hydrolytic breakdown explains the exceptional preservation of ancient peptides.
source: We explain this exceptional preservation in terms of surface stabilization of both the peptide and water molecules involved in the hydrolytic breakdown of the peptide.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic explanation supported by molecular dynamics simulations and experimental data.

claim: Mineral-binding proteins are the most likely source of ancient biomolecular sequences in the fossil record.
source: Our discovery identifies mineral-binding proteins as the most likely source of ancient biomolecular sequences in the fossil record.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The combination of consistency in patterns of protein degradation and survival, independent replication, and in-depth analysis of blanks provides overwhelming evidence for the endogeneity and integrity of the peptides recovered.
source: In this study, we also set out parameters for the authentication of ancient sequences: the combination of the consistency in patterns of protein degradation and survival of particular peptide regions, independent replication of the results and an in-depth analysis of analytical blanks provide overwhelming evidence for the endogeneity and integrity of the peptides recovered.
evidence: This is a summary of the authentication approach used in the study.

claim: All ancient proteomics studies should undertake a similar approach to verify the authenticity of sequences reported.
source: We suggest that all ancient proteomics studies undertake a similar approach to verify the authenticity of the sequences reported.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authentication approach developed in this study.

claim: This study will open up new avenues in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology.
source: We anticipate that this study will open up new avenues in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology, for the first time enabling direct comparison between morphological and molecular records of fossils in deep time.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future impact of the study.

claim: This study enables for the first time direct comparison between morphological and molecular records of fossils in deep time.
source: We anticipate that this study will open up new avenues in palaeontology and palaeoanthropology, for the first time enabling direct comparison between morphological and molecular records of fossils in deep time.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings.

claim: The selective preservation of domains associated with biomineralization offers a novel strategy for uncovering functional regions governing mineral formation.
source: Furthermore, the selective preservation of domains associated with biomineralization offers a novel strategy for uncovering functional regions governing mineral formation.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The intracrystalline fraction of avian eggshell typically contains C-lectins.
source: The intracrystalline fraction of avian eggshell typically contains C-lectins; in ostrich these are struthiocalcin 1 & 2 (SCA-1 & SCA-2) (Mann and Siedler, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mann and Siedler, 2004.

claim: In ostrich eggshell, the C-lectins are struthiocalcin 1 & 2 (SCA-1 & SCA-2).
source: The intracrystalline fraction of avian eggshell typically contains C-lectins; in ostrich these are struthiocalcin 1 & 2 (SCA-1 & SCA-2) (Mann and Siedler, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mann and Siedler, 2004.

claim: The eggshell proteins were characterised in terms of their amino acid composition across microstructural layers.
source: The eggshell proteins were characterised in terms of their amino acid composition across microstructural layers (Appendix 2, sections A and B) and the main proteins sequenced and identified (Appendix 2, section C) in modern eggshell, revealing uniform composition across the eggshell layers.
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 2.

claim: Modern eggshell reveals uniform protein composition across the eggshell layers.
source: The eggshell proteins were characterised in terms of their amino acid composition across microstructural layers (Appendix 2, sections A and B) and the main proteins sequenced and identified (Appendix 2, section C) in modern eggshell, revealing uniform composition across the eggshell layers.
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Samples of archaeological and paleontological eggshell can be considered representative of the overall proteome.
source: Therefore, samples of the archaeological and paleontological eggshell, usually recovered in a fragmentary state, can be considered to be representative of the overall proteome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uniform composition found in modern eggshell.

claim: The crystallography of SCA-1 reveals a similar overall structure to ovocleidin-17 (OC-17).
source: The crystallography of SCA-1 (Ruiz-Arellano et al., 2015) reveals a similar overall structure to ovocleidin-17 (OC-17), which has previously been proposed to play a catalytic role in the calcification of chicken eggshell via the positively charged cluster of arginine residues interacting with the carbonates on the (10.4) calcite surface (Freeman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: OC-17 has been proposed to play a catalytic role in the calcification of chicken eggshell via positively charged arginine residues interacting with carbonates on the calcite surface.
source: The crystallography of SCA-1 (Ruiz-Arellano et al., 2015) reveals a similar overall structure to ovocleidin-17 (OC-17), which has previously been proposed to play a catalytic role in the calcification of chicken eggshell via the positively charged cluster of arginine residues interacting with the carbonates on the (10.4) calcite surface (Freeman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2010.

claim: OC-17 is absent in ostrich.
source: OC-17 is, however, absent in ostrich; instead, SCA-1 and 2 are negatively charged (Table 2) and thus likely to bind to calcium ions.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about ostrich eggshell composition.

claim: SCA-1 and SCA-2 are negatively charged.
source: OC-17 is, however, absent in ostrich; instead, SCA-1 and 2 are negatively charged (Table 2) and thus likely to bind to calcium ions.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: SCA-1 and SCA-2 are likely to bind to calcium ions.
source: OC-17 is, however, absent in ostrich; instead, SCA-1 and 2 are negatively charged (Table 2) and thus likely to bind to calcium ions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative charge of SCA-1 and SCA-2.

claim: Molecular dynamics study identified the strongest binding regions of SCA-1 and SCA-2, two for each protein.
source: A molecular dynamics (MD) study of the binding of whole SCA molecules at the mineral surface allowed the strongest binding regions of SCA-1 and SCA-2 to be identified, two for each of the two proteins (Appendix 3).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data in Appendix 3.

claim: All four peptides covering the binding regions showed negative binding energies.
source: In MD simulations the four peptide sequences that cover the binding regions (Table 2) were moved close to the (10.4) calcite surface from aqueous (bulk) solution to determine their respective binding energies (Appendix 3). All four peptides showed negative binding energies, indicating it was energetically favourable for them to bind to the calcite surface, rather than to remain in solution.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Table 2 and Appendix 3.

claim: Negative binding energies indicate it is energetically favourable for peptides to bind to the calcite surface rather than remain in solution.
source: All four peptides showed negative binding energies, indicating it was energetically favourable for them to bind to the calcite surface, rather than to remain in solution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the binding energy calculations based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: SCA-1 bound more strongly than SCA-2 to the calcite surface.
source: SCA-1 bound more strongly than SCA-2 and the binding energies for all four peptides had the same relative order as in the simulations with full proteins.
evidence: This is supported by binding energy data shown in Table 2.

claim: The binding energies for the four peptides had the same relative order as in the simulations with full proteins.
source: SCA-1 bound more strongly than SCA-2 and the binding energies for all four peptides had the same relative order as in the simulations with full proteins.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of binding energy data in Table 2.

claim: The peptides operate as effective proxies for the binding of SCA.
source: This indicates that the peptides operate as effective proxies for the binding of SCA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of binding patterns between peptides and full proteins.

claim: The differences between bindings of different peptides are probably due to individual amino acids and the primary structure enabling favoured binding configurations.
source: The differences between bindings of the different peptides are probably due to the individual amino acids and the primary structure of the peptide enabling favoured binding configurations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the molecular basis for differential binding.

claim: When a molecule binds at the surface there will be an entropy loss for the molecule as it becomes bound.
source: When a molecule binds at the surface there will also be changes in entropy - an entropy loss for the molecule as it becomes bound and an entropy gain as water molecules on the surface are displaced.
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: When a molecule binds at the surface there will be an entropy gain as water molecules on the surface are displaced.
source: When a molecule binds at the surface there will also be changes in entropy - an entropy loss for the molecule as it becomes bound and an entropy gain as water molecules on the surface are displaced.
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: The displacement of multiple water molecules when one molecule binds is an entropically favourable process.
source: Given only one molecule binds, compared to the displacement of multiple water molecules, this will be an entropically favourable process.
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic principles regarding entropy changes.

claim: The estimated free energy values demonstrate the same trends as the configurational energy.
source: These estimated free energy values (including the influence of water displacement) demonstrate the same trends as the configurational energy, since the number of water molecules displaced in all cases is similar.
evidence: This is supported by free energy calculations shown in Table 2.

claim: The number of water molecules displaced is similar in all cases.
source: These estimated free energy values (including the influence of water displacement) demonstrate the same trends as the configurational energy, since the number of water molecules displaced in all cases is similar.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: Water close to the interface is more ordered than bulk water and has lower energy.
source: The structure of the water close to the interface is also more ordered than bulk water and has lower energy.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulations and established knowledge about interfacial water.

claim: When hydrolysis of the bound protein or peptide occurs, it must react with the stabilized water at the interface, not the water in the bulk.
source: Thus, when hydrolysis of the bound protein or peptide occurs, it must react with the stabilized water at the interface, not the water in the bulk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of bound peptides at the mineral surface.

claim: Reacting with stabilized water at the interface will raise the barrier to hydrolysis and promote sequence survival.
source: This will raise the barrier to hydrolysis and thus promote the survival of the sequence (see also the discussion below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the stabilization of interfacial water.

claim: The stronger the peptide binding, the more likely the sequence is to survive in the fossil record.
source: We would therefore expect that the stronger the peptide binding, the more likely the sequence is to survive in the fossil record, as it is best stabilized by its interactions with the mineral surface and must react with stabilized water.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism of preservation.

claim: The MD simulations predict that the YSALDDDDYPKG sequence will survive the longest.
source: The MD simulations thus predict that the YSALDDDDYPKG sequence, with the lowest binding energy (Table 2) will survive the longest.
evidence: This is a prediction based on binding energy calculations shown in Table 2.

claim: The YSALDDDDYPKG sequence has the lowest binding energy.
source: The MD simulations thus predict that the YSALDDDDYPKG sequence, with the lowest binding energy (Table 2) will survive the longest.
evidence: This is supported by binding energy data shown in Table 2.

claim: Twenty-four eggshell samples were sourced from well-dated sites in South Africa and Tanzania.
source: Twenty-four eggshell samples were sourced from well-dated sites in South Africa and Tanzania (Figure 1, Table 1): Elands Bay Cave (0.3–16 ka BP, Table 3), Pinnacle Point Caves PP 5/6 and PP 30 (50–80 ka BP and ~150 ka BP, respectively, Table 4), Wonderwerk Cave (1 Ma, Table 5), Olduvai Gorge (1.34 Ma, Table 6) and Laetoli (2.6–4.3 Ma, Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by site information in Tables 1, 3-7.

claim: The age and stratigraphy of the oldest fossils from Laetoli is well-constrained despite the eggshell fragments being surface finds.
source: The age and stratigraphy of the oldest fossils, from Laetoli, is well-constrained despite the eggshell fragments being surface finds: their morphology shows no evidence of long-distance transport and the fossil-bearing horizons are well identified within the stratigraphy.
evidence: This is an assessment of the geological context of the Laetoli samples.

claim: The morphology of Laetoli eggshell fragments shows no evidence of long-distance transport.
source: The age and stratigraphy of the oldest fossils, from Laetoli, is well-constrained despite the eggshell fragments being surface finds: their morphology shows no evidence of long-distance transport and the fossil-bearing horizons are well identified within the stratigraphy.
evidence: This is based on morphological examination of the samples.

claim: The fossil-bearing horizons at Laetoli are well identified within the stratigraphy.
source: The age and stratigraphy of the oldest fossils, from Laetoli, is well-constrained despite the eggshell fragments being surface finds: their morphology shows no evidence of long-distance transport and the fossil-bearing horizons are well identified within the stratigraphy.
evidence: This is based on stratigraphic analysis of the site.

claim: The absence of lava flows in stratigraphic proximity excludes the possibility that Laetoli eggshell fragments had been exposed to additional heat.
source: The absence of lava flows in stratigraphic proximity also excludes the possibility that these fragments had been exposed to additional heat.
evidence: This is based on geological assessment of the site stratigraphy.

claim: The provenance of the fragments from Olduvai Gorge is secure.
source: The provenance of the fragments from Olduvai Gorge is also secure, as these were found in situ during the excavation of the Bell Korongo site, which overlies directly a volcanic tuff dated by 40Ar/39Ar (Domínguez-Rodrigo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the archaeological context and dating of the site.

claim: Olduvai eggshell fragments were found in situ during excavation of the Bell Korongo site.
source: The provenance of the fragments from Olduvai Gorge is also secure, as these were found in situ during the excavation of the Bell Korongo site, which overlies directly a volcanic tuff dated by 40Ar/39Ar (Domínguez-Rodrigo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the archaeological excavation record.

claim: The Bell Korongo site overlies directly a volcanic tuff dated by 40Ar/39Ar.
source: The provenance of the fragments from Olduvai Gorge is also secure, as these were found in situ during the excavation of the Bell Korongo site, which overlies directly a volcanic tuff dated by 40Ar/39Ar (Domínguez-Rodrigo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Domínguez-Rodrigo et al., 2013.

claim: The intracrystalline proteome composition in modern eggshell does not vary across microstructural layers.
source: The intracrystalline proteome composition in modern eggshell does not vary across microstructural layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but patterns of degradation are different between fossil samples and purified proteins degraded at high temperature in the absence of the mineral (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patterns of degradation are different between fossil samples and purified proteins degraded at high temperature in the absence of the mineral.
source: The intracrystalline proteome composition in modern eggshell does not vary across microstructural layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but patterns of degradation are different between fossil samples and purified proteins degraded at high temperature in the absence of the mineral (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
